callouts.label: Hand Crank
callouts.hint: A small L-shaped handle with a round wooden knob, sticking out of the side of the box at the lower left.
callouts.description: The crank on the side of the box drove everything. Turn it forward and the dials showed the sky on a future date; turn it back and they showed a past one. Its answer was the same for everyone who turned it, rich or poor, king or farmer. And its answer was fixed before the event, so it could be checked: an eclipse happens or it does not. On our route: Day 13, the National Archaeological Museum, where the surviving device is kept.
callouts.tip: The Antikythera Gears MicroSim shows how tooth counts turn one crank into different speeds. Its ratios are simplified for teaching and do not reconstruct the real mechanism.

callouts.label: The Gear Train
callouts.hint: A dense stack of small and large toothed bronze wheels meshing inside the open wooden box.
callouts.description: Inside the wooden box, a train of at least 30 gears cut by hand from thin bronze sheet turned the crank into pointer motion. The gears were cut with small triangular teeth, and X-ray scans made in 2005 let researchers count teeth hidden inside the corroded lumps. The hardest part was the Moon, which moves faster in some parts of its orbit than others. The maker used two slightly off-center gears linked by a pin sliding in a slot. The evidence points to a workshop, quite possibly on Rhodes, using the lunar theory of Hipparchus. On our route: Day 13, and Day 8 at Rhodes, where the workshop may have stood.

callouts.label: Zodiac and Calendar Rings
callouts.hint: Two concentric rings of fine tick marks around the edge of the large round dial on the left.
callouts.description: The front dial has a zodiac ring and a calendar ring. They answer the first question an owner could ask: where are the Sun and the Moon among the stars on this date? The cycles set into the gears are the solar year and the Moon's monthly circuit. The calendar ring follows the 365-day Egyptian civil calendar, with the Egyptian month names inscribed. In modern reconstructions the front also shows the five planets known to the Greeks. On our route: Day 13.
callouts.tip: Planets appear in modern reconstructions of the front dial, as the appendix notes.

callouts.label: Moon-Phase Ball
callouts.hint: A small round ball in a window near the top of the big dial, with one half silver and the other half black.
callouts.description: A small ball, half silver and half black, turned to show the phase of the Moon. It answered the question: what will the Moon look like that night? The cycle behind it is the month from new moon to new moon. Making a ball that turned to show phases was one of the mechanical designs the workshop had to master. The Antikythera Gears MicroSim leaves lunar phases out, so this is a part of the machine the sim does not cover. On our route: Day 13.

callouts.label: Metonic Spiral
callouts.hint: A flat bronze panel on the back with a spiral groove of five turns winding in toward its center.
callouts.description: A spiral of 235 lunar months keeps the Moon's calendar in step with the solar year. The Greeks found that 19 years and 235 lunar months differ by only about two hours, so after 19 years the Moon's phases fall on nearly the same calendar dates again. Because 235 is 5 × 47, the dial is a spiral of five turns with 47 months on each turn. It answered: which month of the calendar is it? The month names come from a real Greek city's calendar. On our route: Day 13.

callouts.label: Games Dial
callouts.hint: A small round dial at the right edge of the upper back panel, divided into four equal sections.
callouts.description: The games dial shows which athletic festivals fell in each year of a four-year cycle, including the Olympic Games. It answered: are the Olympic Games this year? A damaged name on this dial has been read by the classicist Paul Iversen as the Halieia, the games Rhodes held for its sun god Helios. That is one reason Rhodes is a leading candidate for where the device was made. On our route: Day 13, with Rhodes on Day 8.
callouts.tip: Where it was made is argued. The calendar on the Metonic dial uses month names from the family of Corinth and its colonies, which points elsewhere.

callouts.label: Saros Eclipse Spiral
callouts.hint: A flat bronze panel at the lower back with a long spiral groove, its cells marked with small symbols.
callouts.description: The lower back spiral of 223 lunar months predicts eclipses. This is the Saros, about 18 years, a cycle Babylonian astronomers found from centuries of nightly records. A symbol on each month marked one that would have a solar or lunar eclipse. Because 223 is a prime number, it cannot be built from smaller gears, so the mechanism has a gear with 223 teeth. It answered: could there be an eclipse that month, and at about what hour? On our route: Day 13.
callouts.tip: A Babylonian clay tablet listing eclipse months counts the same cycle. The method, not the material, makes it a cycle model.

callouts.label: Exeligmos Dial
callouts.hint: A small round dial next to the lower spiral, divided into three sections.
callouts.description: A Saros is about eight hours longer than a whole number of days, so each repeat of an eclipse happens about eight hours later in the day. The small exeligmos dial, marked for 0, 8, and 16 hours, tells the user how much to add to the eclipse time. Three Saros cycles, 54 years, bring an eclipse back to nearly the same hour. On our route: Day 13.

callouts.label: Surviving Fragments
callouts.hint: A few lumpy, green-brown corroded pieces of metal lying on the ground, one with a gear edge showing.
callouts.description: What survives is 82 fragments holding at least 30 gears, not a finished machine. In 1900 sponge divers sheltering from a storm off Antikythera found a Roman-era shipwreck that had sunk about 70 to 60 BCE. No one noticed the corroded lump until 1902, when the archaeologist Valerios Stais saw a gear wheel in a broken piece. The device itself is from the 2nd century BCE. In 1959 Derek de Solla Price called it "an ancient Greek computer." On our route: Day 13, the National Archaeological Museum.
callouts.tip: Do not picture a general-purpose computer. Its answers were fixed in its gears when it was made, and a wrong ratio stayed wrong.
